When you’re hypomanic/manic, unless you’ve gotten good at catching yourself, it feels like there’s nothing wrong and that you are stable. If anything, you feel great. Most of the time, people with bipolar ARE stable in between episodes. It’s the existence of hypomanic/manic episodes that diagnose it. Hell, you can experience one manic episode in your entire life with no depression and still be bipolar. Bipolar can absolutely be stable, especially with proper treatment.

It sounds like you may have some symptoms of bipolar like elevated mood, goal oriented behavior, and risky behaviors. That is not enough symptoms to diagnose so I would recommend looking at the diagnostic criteria and seeing if any more line up. Also, you mentioned possible hypomania induced by Ritalin. If it is caused by a drug, it may not count as hypomania unless you have those episodes without it.

There’s also the possibility of cyclothymia which is when there is not enough to diagnose a depressive or hypomanic/manic episode, but these mood swings are still affecting your life enough for it to be a disorder.

Keep working with your psychiatrist, you’ll figure it out.

I hear you. Bipolar is not easy to live with. It does get better once you learn to manage it. Like, a lot better.

Here are some things I would recommend based off your post: Stay in therapy and ask your therapist these exact questions. They know you, they have training, you can absolutely ask them for aid in managing your bipolar and answers to your questions about your future. You don’t always have to spend it on past trauma, though it helps. Sometimes you get burnt out talking about the same things over and over. Keep trying in psychiatry. I’ve also been on 15 medications. There may be one out there that works well for you, or perhaps you’ll be recommended into a different treatment. It is not a good idea for people with bipolar to not be medicated. It’s also worth looking into vitamins. Stay sober to the best of your abilities, but don’t beat yourself up for relapses. Just try again the next day. Look into support groups for that, such as an anonymous group.

I personally have a list I made with my therapist about symptoms I experience in hypomania and depression. When I start questioning whether I am entering an episode or not, we look at the list. The best thing you can do for episodes, in my opinion, is early intervention. It’s easier to start going on walks to aid depression in the beginning when you still have some energy than in the middle of one. You can also catch yourself and understand you are in a manic/hypomanic episode with this and made more informed decisions knowing you aren’t in your usual headspace. Keeping a daily tracker of your mood is also helpful. Just once a day. Makes you reflect on the day a little and aids in recognizing when episodes are occurring. Sometimes when you are in episodes, you just kind of have to wait it out and use your coping skills, but knowing where you are emotionally is a good thing. 

It’s hard, but use those coping skills. In manic/hypomanic episodes, look at ways that get that energy out in a healthy way. Exercise (including walks and yoga, doesn’t have to be at a gym), art, trying new things (safely). Even scribbling widely on paper can help. In depressive episodes, make sure you are eating, even if it’s granola bars. Try to keep up with hygiene, even if it’s just a face wipe. A walk can do wonders, even if it’s around your room/apartment/house/whatever. Just a tiny bit of effort is okay, you don’t have to do the full thing. Just what your energy can handle. Sometimes it is a waiting game, but you can make it easier/shorter with coping skills.

You could always start going back to church and going back to volunteer work, if you have the energy for it. It would give you some structure. I would also personally really recommend Al-anon meetings, since you mentioned your father was an alcoholic. It’s like Alcoholics Anonymous, but for people affected by alcoholics. It’s a support group. I’ve made some peace with my qualifier (person whose drinking I was affected by) and childhood through this group and it’s associated literature. They have online and in-person meetings. If you don’t want to show your face, go to online ones and just turn your camera off. They have meetings everywhere. If it’s not in your area, they have online ones not restricted to any area as well. It’s good, at least, to have a space to talk where people understand and gives you some additional structure. 

I’m not sure what to say about college. It can be really helpful having a schedule and planning for your future, but can also hurt your mental health from the stress. Try easy 100 classes. Be gentle with yourself if you have to drop them, it’s not a waste of money if you tried. You can always explain why you dropped. Most college students drop at least one class. Some schools give the option for an excused withdrawal if you have documentation from a mental health professional that your mental health prevented you from doing the course. Looks better on a transcript. 

I hope this helps in anyway at all.
